D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.status: FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-30, in the same cycle. Found by chasing an anomaly instead of accepting a convenient number; the fix is shipped, proven red by reproducing the original defect, and the population it silently dropped is restored.
D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.what:
`selection_rate.derive()` built its `scenario id -> expect_tool` map from the scenario files AS THEY ARE NOW, while counting runs recorded weeks earlier. Retiring or renaming a scenario id therefore removed every historical run of it from the DENOMINATOR, with no error and no log line — the rate simply moved.

The DQ-T50 both-arms split retired `composition-glossary-build-with-an-ontology`, replacing it with two better-designed arms. Entirely correct, and the side effect was:

    composition_build_cast_and_graph   30/125 = 0.24   before
                                       35/70  = 0.50   after the rename
                                       60/155 = 0.387  with history restored

The denominator SHRANK from 125 to 70 while the corpus only grew. 117 non-errored runs across 5 scenario ids were orphaned — outside every denominator in the contract.
D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.why_it_matters:
🔴 IT REACHES VERDICTS. DQ-T51's reachability bar (0.4507) decides whether `called 0/5` is read as evidence about a TOOL or as a lost draw, and 0.24 -> 0.50 moved this tool ACROSS it. A scenario rename could change how a zero-call batch is judged, in either direction, with no behaviour having changed.

AND IT AGREED WITH WHAT I ALREADY BELIEVED, which is what makes it worth a row rather than a line in a commit. The apparent rise looked like corpus-wide corroboration of the measured inversion on D-A-HOT-SET-INCUMBENT-WITH-A-RECIPE-BEATS-AN-R1-FORCED-CHALLENGER — the challenger being picked more often everywhere. I was one step from quoting it as evidence. The restored figure says the opposite: corpus-wide the challenger is picked in 39% of runs that expect it, which is not a tool that has started winning everywhere.
D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.how_it_was_found:
Re-running the deriver after a batch showed exactly one tool leaving the lottery band. The cheap reading was 'the inversion is showing up in the corpus'. The check that refuted it was arithmetic: the tool's RUN COUNT had fallen from 125 to 70 while the corpus only ever grows. A denominator that shrinks is not a behaviour change.

The first hypothesis was wrong too and is recorded: that two scenario files declared the same id with different `expect_tool` and a first-wins `setdefault` picked the wrong one. Measured across every scenario file — ZERO ids declare more than one tool. The real cause was an id that no file declares AT ALL any more.
D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.the_fix:
contracts/scenario-expect-tool-history.json — append-only `id -> tool`, seeded by reading every version of every scenarios-*.json across 324 commits (311 ids recovered). `selection_rate._history()` supplies it; CURRENT declarations still win, so a deliberately changed expect_tool still takes effect and history only answers for ids nobody declares any more.

`_append_history()` runs with the deriver and folds every declared id in WHILE IT IS STILL DECLARED, which is what stops the fix decaying: the git recovery was a one-off, the append is the mechanism. Nothing is ever removed — an id leaving the scenario files is exactly the id whose meaning must survive.

`unmapped_runs()` reports runs that map to no tool, and the deriver PRINTS the count, so the next orphan is loud instead of silent. 117 -> 5.
D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.red_able:
scripts/test_a_scenario_rename_cannot_rewrite_a_measured_rate.py, 6 guards. Proven red by REPRODUCING THE ORIGINAL DEFECT rather than by a synthetic edit: the retired id was dropped from the history contract, and two guards went red — the orphan count rose and the tool's restored denominator collapsed again. Restored byte-identical, sha256 c76635793ebe16bb9da9a5722e4efd48748044950dc9f42fb73a5020a0eaaebc.

Includes an anti-vacuity guard, because `unmapped_runs()` returning {} for reading nothing would satisfy the orphan bar forever, and this loop has drawn a conclusion from a silently-empty capture before.
D-A-SCENARIO-RENAME-SILENTLY-REWRITES-A-.what_is_NOT_covered:
- FIVE RUNS ARE STILL ORPHANED (`glossary-build-is-it-in-the-catalogue`). No commit declares an `expect_tool` for it, so there is nothing to recover; it is below MIN_RUNS and cannot move a rate. It is NAMED in the guard's baseline rather than rounded into a tolerance, so a later orphan shows up as an increase.
- THE OTHER DERIVED CONTRACTS WERE NOT AUDITED for the same shape. Any instrument that joins historical run records to CURRENT declarations can be rewritten by a refactor the same way; only selection_rate was checked.
- NO CLAIM THAT PAST VERDICTS WERE WRONG. The bar classifies the same 22 tools before and after the fix, so no conclusion on disk is known to have turned on this. That is luck rather than design — the artefact was large enough to cross the bar, and it happened to be caught in the same session it was introduced.

D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.status: OPEN, found 2026-08-30 by a corpus guard going red. The FALSE FLAG it produced is cleared and quarantined to one named session; the race underneath it is not fixed and the cause is not known.
D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.what:
`fe_runner` takes the DATA bar's `before` snapshot immediately after the fixture is built and seed-asserted, and its docstring says why: 'if the seed were inside the before/after window, every scenario would report a store change and the DATA bar would be meaningless'. The ordering is right. But the store still moves BETWEEN that snapshot and the turn.

Measured on session 01a04fe3-bd8e-7d21-81f2-4555c920a8c7 (c-silenttrigger2, composition-arc-get-v2 rep 4):

    before  loreweave_composition.composition_work  rows=1  latest=23:38:22.478817
    after                                           rows=1  latest=23:38:37.437706
    the book's ONLY work row: created_at == updated_at = 23:38:37.437706
    the turn's FIRST chat message                          = 23:38:40.448765

`snapshot()` scopes composition_work by book_id, so rows=1 on both sides with a moved `latest` means the row was REPLACED — one existed at 23:38:22, and the one there now was created at 23:38:37, three seconds BEFORE the model was asked anything.
D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.why_it_matters:
The DATA bar reads `store_diff` as 'what this TURN changed'. If the baseline is not the state the turn starts from, that reading is wrong in both directions: it can attribute a pre-turn write to the model — which is exactly what happened here, flagging a READ-intent scenario as a lifecycle write — and it can hide a real write that merely restores a value.

The false direction is the one caught, and it is the more dangerous one for this loop: a read tool appearing to write is precisely the kind of finding that gets filed as a defect against the platform. It took the store's own timestamps to refute it.
D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.how_to_reproduce: Rare — ONE run in a corpus of 213 raw files, and 100+ read-intent runs pass the same guard. Compare, for a flagged run: the row's created_at in the owning DB against the session's first chat_messages.created_at. A created_at that predates the turn is the signature.
D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.what_is_NOT_known:
- WHAT REPLACES THE ROW. Nothing in the measured window should touch composition_work between `assert_seeded` and the first user message. Candidates not tested: a lazy composition-work creation on the read path itself (which would make this a PLATFORM row, not an instrument one), a second provisioning step, or another concurrent repeat writing through a shared resolver. Concurrency was 1 for this batch, which weakens the last of those.
- WHETHER IT IS SPECIFIC TO composition_work. Seven other tables in the same run carry `after: None`, so they could not have shown it either way.
- 🔴 WHETHER OTHER FLAGS IN THE CORPUS WERE THE SAME THING. This is the first one caught. Earlier false flags on this guard were diagnosed differently and are not re-opened here.
D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.the_flag_is_quarantined_not_excused: scripts/test_a_read_audit_row_is_not_a_lifecycle_write.py carries the session id in a one-entry exception set with the clearing arithmetic written beside it, plus a guard that FAILS if the set ever grows — because a second instance means the race is recurring and wants fixing, not listing. The exception is keyed on the SESSION ID, not on the scenario or the table, so it cannot quietly cover the next one.
D-THE-BEFORE-SNAPSHOT-IS-NOT-THE-STATE-T.my_recommendation: Take the `before` snapshot as late as possible — immediately before the first user message is sent rather than immediately after seeding — and record that timestamp on the run. Runs carry no turn-start time today (`started_at` is None on every record), which is why refuting this single flag needed a live DB query instead of the run file. With the timestamp recorded, the detector could reject any change whose `latest` predates the turn without any exception list at all. NOT MY CALL to reshape the measured unit — the current ordering is deliberate and documented — so this is a recommendation, and the row stays open.

D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.status: OPEN and blocked on DQ-T74. Found 2026-08-30 by asking how a `proven` delete tool could have 658 blank-argument calls. Measured over the whole corpus, with the two obvious innocent explanations tested and refuted. Changing 17 tools' state is the owner's call, not mine.
D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.what:
SEVENTEEN tools carry `state: proven` in this ledger and have NEVER ONCE returned `ok: true` in any recorded run. Not once, in 376 calls:

    world_map_create               77      composition_derivative_edit        9
    world_map_add_marker           53      composition_conformance_run        6
    composition_arc_template_edit  52      composition_authoring_run_review   6
    world_map_delete               50      kg_entity_edge_timeline            5
    composition_reference_update   26      registry_get_workflow              5
    composition_motif_bind_edit    21      jobs_cancel                        5
    glossary_entity_restore        20      composition_arc_import_analyze     1
    catalog_get_book               18      settings_model_set_active         12
    plan_keep_material             10

Every one of those 376 calls is an outright ERROR. The dominant error is a missing required id — "'world_map_delete' is missing required argument(s): ['map_id']" — with a minority of domain refusals (registry_get_workflow: 'workflow not found', composition_derivative_edit: 'NOT_A_DERIVATIVE').
D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.the_two_innocent_explanations_were_TESTE:
This looked too large to be true, so both benign readings were measured rather than assumed.

🔴 1 — 'THEY ARE TIER-A TOOLS THAT CORRECTLY STOP AT A CONFIRM CARD.' A carded call is `ok:false` and the gate explicitly counts it as success: 'a gated proposal (a confirm card) counts: the tool ran and its gate held'. If the harness never approves, a legitimate write tool would look exactly like this. Classified all 376 results into ok / carded / errored:

    ok 0    carded 0    errored 376

ZERO carded. Not one of these tools ever reached a confirm card. The explanation is refuted for all seventeen.

🔴 2 — 'THE EVIDENCE POINTER IS JUST BADLY CHOSEN; THEY SUCCEED IN OTHER BATCHES.' The sweep was widened from the cited evidence file to EVERY raw record on disk. That control WORKED and is why the number is 17 and not 19: `jobs_get` (69 ok of 130) and `translation_patch_block` (8 of 20) do succeed elsewhere and were removed. The remaining seventeen have no success anywhere.
D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.why_it_matters:
`proven` is the verdict every other conclusion in this ledger leans on, and 17 of them mean 'the model reached for this tool and the harness did not crash'. The LIVE bar is literally `called >= 1` with zero errored RUNS — a run errors when the HARNESS fails, not when the tool returns an error — so a tool the model calls and that refuses every single time passes it.

This is the same distinction the selection-rate work drew for reachability ('proven over a 1-in-50 tool and a 50-in-50 tool are not the same sentence') applied one level deeper: proven REACHABLE is not proven FUNCTIONAL, and the ledger uses one word for both.

It also explains a puzzle on another row. D-BLANK-ARGS-CONCENTRATES-WHERE-NO-AMBIENT-ID-EXISTS found 658 blank-argument calls on world/map tools whose supplier was advertised ZERO times, and every one of those tools is `proven`. Both facts are true because the verdict never asked whether the call worked.
D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.what_is_NOT_claimed:
- NOT that these tools are BROKEN. Most fail for a missing required id, which is the supplier gap (D-A-REQUIRED-ID-NEEDS-ITS-SUPPLIER-ON-THE-SAME-SURFACE), not a fault in the tool. Called with the right arguments they may work perfectly; a direct probe would likely show that, and several have `ship_exercised` evidence from exactly such a probe.
- NOT that the bar was applied wrongly. It was applied exactly as written. The defect is in what the word promises, not in anyone's diligence.
- 🔴 ONLY 40 OF 204 PROVEN TOOLS COULD BE CHECKED AT ALL — the rest have no readable raw file beside their cited evidence, so the true figure is unknown and 17 is a FLOOR over the checkable fifth.
- `ok` is read from the recorded TOOL_CALL_RESULT payload. A tool whose result omits `ok` would be miscounted; none of the 376 did — the `other/unparsed` bucket is 0 for all 17.
D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.my_recommendation:
NOT MY CALL — it would re-open 17 verdicts, which is exactly the kind of by-side-effect reclassification this loop refuses to make on its own. Filed as DQ-T74.

What I would recommend: keep `proven` meaning what it means and make it SAY so, rather than demoting 17 rows. The gate already knows the numbers — add the outcome to the verdict line the way the selection rate was added, so a reader is handed 'proven (reachable; 0 of 50 calls returned ok)' instead of a bare 'proven'. That is cheap, changes no state, and makes the silent half audible. Demoting the rows is the alternative and it is more disruptive.
D-SEVENTEEN-PROVEN-TOOLS-HAVE-NEVER-ONCE.red_able: NOT BUILT — deliberately. A guard asserting '17 tools have zero successes' would freeze the defect as a baseline, and the right fix changes the number. The measurement is reproducible from the corpus in one sweep and is recorded above with its two refuted controls.

DQ-T1.question: What is `entity_lifecycle_ledger` for, and what should write it? Options seen, none chosen: (a) every status transition (approve/retire/reject via glossary_propose_curation) appends a row, making the ledger the audit trail its columns describe; (b) it is delete/restore-only by design and the column set is aspirational; (c) it is superseded by entity_revisions and should be dropped.
DQ-T1.evidence: Measured 2026-08-13. The table exists with an append-only trigger guard (`entity_lifecycle_ledger_append_only`) and columns op, prior_status, new_status, actor_type, actor_id, reason — the exact vocabulary of a curation status change. It holds THREE rows, all from 2026-08-11, all op='deleted'/'restored', and all with prior_status and new_status NULL. A repo-wide search for 'lifecycle_ledger' finds NOTHING in source, and the only database function referencing it is the append-only guard. Four entities were moved draft -> active live in this cycle and the ledger gained no rows. So it is a table with a guard, no writer, and a column set that describes a transition nobody records. Whether curation SHOULD write it is a product decision about what the audit trail is for, not something measurement can settle.
DQ-T1.recommendation: RECOMMEND (a) - every status transition appends. Not because the ledger is used, but because somebody paid for an append-only TRIGGER on it: that is a deliberate integrity guarantee, and a guarded table holding three rows from a single day is the shape that later gets read as an audit trail it never was. (c) drop-it is the honest alternative and is cheaper; what makes it the wrong DEFAULT is that the columns (op, prior_status, new_status, actor_type, actor_id, reason) already describe the curation transition exactly, so the intent is not in doubt. Decide (c) only after checking for readers - if anything reads it today, (c) is a silent capability loss.

DQ-T2.question: Should a deprecated tool be required to name a replacement, and what replaces the ones that have none? Options seen, none chosen: (a) superseded_by becomes mandatory for visibility=legacy and the 55 gaps are filled; (b) a retired-with-no-successor tool is legitimate and tool_list's description should stop promising a label; (c) those 55 are not actually deprecated and the visibility tag is wrong.
DQ-T2.evidence: Measured 2026-08-13 against the live federated catalogue. 117 tools carry _meta.visibility='legacy'; 62 carry superseded_by and 55 DO NOT, spread across five services (glossary 28, book 11, kg 11, lore 4, composition 1). tool_list's own description says 'deprecated tools are labeled with their replacement', so for 47% of them there is no label. Observed live in session 019ff9f0: asked what replaced book_get, the model built an accurate migration table for the tools that name a successor and could say nothing actionable about book_create, book_chapter_delete, book_purge or book_set_cover. This is not tool_list's defect - it reports the _meta each provider federates faithfully - and whether a retired tool HAS a successor is a product decision per tool, not something measurement can settle.
DQ-T2.recommendation: RECOMMEND (a) - superseded_by mandatory for visibility=legacy, the 55 gaps filled, enforced by a lint. tool_list's own description PROMISES the label, and 55 of 117 legacy tools do not carry it, so the promise is false for nearly half of them. (b) 'stop promising it' is internally consistent but trades a fixable data gap for a permanent capability loss - the successor is exactly what a model needs when it lands on a legacy tool. The enforcement shape already exists: scripts/lint_superseded_synonyms.py fails the pair at build.

DQ-T3.question: Should tool_list tell the model that world-setup tools exist but are withheld? Options seen, none chosen: (a) stamp them the way T7-D2 stamps always-on tools, naming the gate and how to open it; (b) keep them wholly invisible, since naming a tool the model cannot call is the retry loop N5a-FULL exists to stop; (c) widen the exemption so a direct request counts as setup intent.
DQ-T3.evidence: Measured 2026-08-13. filter_intent_gated_setup_tools drops five glossary tools (adopt_standards, propose_kinds, plan, propose_batch, book_sync_apply) at catalog assembly unless the glossary_shaping skill is injected or a pinned rail names them - so they are un-seeded, un-findable AND un-loadable. That is deliberate (N5a-FULL, the confirmed over-reach) and it IS instrumented via record_surface_withheld(stage='intent_gate'), but only into telemetry the model never sees: from the model's side they are indistinguishable from tools that do not exist. The gate's own docstring records the cost of the opposite error - guidance naming a tool the capability floor had made unreachable produced 40,597 characters of one repeated paragraph before the author hit Stop. So both directions have a measured failure and the choice is a product decision.
DQ-T3.decision: ANSWERED 2026-08-14 by the owner: option (a) — stamp withheld tools the way T7-D2 stamps always-on ones, naming the gate and how to open it. NOTE FOR WHOEVER BUILDS IT: three prose interventions were measured this session and none moved tool_list off 0/3, so the prior is against prose working here. Build it and MEASURE it; if the measurement refuses it, say so rather than shipping it.
DQ-T3.recommendation: RECOMMEND (b) - keep them wholly invisible, and fix the GATE instead (DQ-T31). Naming a tool the model cannot call is the retry loop N5a-FULL exists to stop. The reason a user's request cannot reach an intent-gated tool is not that the tool is hidden; it is that the gate keys on vocabulary rather than on what was asked. Fix that and (a) stops being needed. DECIDE THESE TWO TOGETHER: (b) here is only defensible if T31 gets its declaration arm - otherwise the tools are both unreachable and unmentioned.

DQ-T5.question: How does a NEW book get its first glossary entity? Options seen, none chosen: (a) let a refusal UNLOCK the tool it names for the rest of the turn, the way a pinned rail's step tools are already exempted from the intent gate; (b) make the router inject glossary_shaping on prose like 'set up my book, adopt the standard lore categories', which it does not today; (c) let glossary_ontology_upsert create a kind that is actually usable (with a display attribute), so the non-gated path works end to end; (d) bootstrap a default ontology with the book, the way a knowledge project is already bootstrapped 197ms after creation (OBS-T17).
DQ-T5.evidence: Measured live 2026-08-13 across sessions 019ffa85, 019ffa92 and 019ffa96 on a throwaway book, with every branch tried. A fresh book has no kinds, so glossary_propose_entities refuses. Its remedy, glossary_adopt_standards, is intent-gated and was recorded WITHHELD at stage=intent_gate in the same turn as the refusal that named it - and stayed withheld even on the explicit prose 'Set up my book - adopt the standard lore categories for it'. The non-gated alternative, glossary_ontology_upsert, DOES create the kind (confirmed in the store) but the kind has no display attribute, so the propose is correctly refused with 'refusing to create a nameless entity'; adding a name attribute through the same tool returned ok and changed nothing - the retry produced a byte-identical refusal. Both directions have a measured cost: opening the gate re-admits the over-reach N5a-FULL exists to stop (its docstring records 40,597 characters of one repeated paragraph before the author hit Stop), and leaving it shut means the glossary has no entry point for a new book. Measurement can show the contradiction; it cannot choose which side is intended.
DQ-T5.recommendation: RECOMMEND (a) - a refusal UNLOCKS the tool it names, for the rest of that turn. The platform already does exactly this for a pinned rail's step tools, so the mechanism exists and only its trigger is new; and a refusal naming its own remedy is the strongest evidence of intent available - the system itself just said which tool is needed. It is reactive rather than pre-emptive, which is the pattern that has held up elsewhere here. DQ-T33.mechanism_now_known_2026_08_24:
THE DECISION HAS A MECHANISM UNDER IT NOW, WHICH SPLITS IT IN TWO. It was posed as 'what does the service show the author when a turn says nothing' - one question, answerable only in the abstract because the silence had no known cause. It now has one:

The model abandons the structured tool-call channel and emits ONLY the closing control token `<tool_call|>`. There is no call to salvage. The hold that would have caught it is keyed on the OPENING token, a different string, so the delimiter flushes into the reasoning channel and the pass ends as an ordinary 'stopped without a tool call'. `_is_bare_toolcall_marker_only` now names that state, with 14 tests and a proven-RED falsifier.

SO THERE ARE TWO SEPARABLE QUESTIONS, and only the second is really a product one:

  (a) WHAT THE SERVICE DOES. The model's INTENT was a tool call - it emitted the delimiter for one. Retrying that pass is ordinary engineering on a degenerate generation, not a choice about what the assistant may say. DQ-T39.measured:

LIVE: registry_list_workflows surfaced 5/5 and was called 0/5 — the model chose workflow_list every time and ANSWERED WELL, with an accurate rundown of the recipes and their slugs. On the evidence the model's choice is the RIGHT one: workflow_list is the half of the pair wired to workflow_load(slug), which is how a workflow is actually run.

Answerability is not the mechanism: registry_list_workflows is the ONLY answerable tool on that prompt (set size 1). workflow_list reaches the wire as a consumer-local tool, which answerability never sees, so no synonym or precedence expressed through answerability can reach this pair.
DQ-T39.why_it_is_a_decision: The platform already has the mechanism — drop_superseded_tools removes a legacy tool from the turn catalogue when its replacement is on the same wire, and it withholds 83 today. The alternative — retiring workflow_list and routing the runner through the federated tool — is a bigger change for no measured gain, since nothing is currently broken for the AUTHOR: they get a good answer either way. DQ-T39.THE_PREMISE_I_PUT_UP_WAS_WRONG_2026_08_2:

WHAT I CLAIMED: 'registry_list_workflows and workflow_list answer the same request and return the same shape.' I compared their DESCRIPTIONS and their RETURN SHAPES. Same shape is true. Same job is false, and the difference is scope:

    workflow_list           -> workflows_client.get_workflows(user_id, book_id=…,
                                   surface=…, mode=permission_mode)
                               i.e. what is loadable ON THIS SURFACE, FOR THIS BOOK,
                               IN THIS MODE — turn-scoped
    registry_list_workflows -> 'the curated multi-step workflows visible to the signed-in
                               user' — user-scoped, no surface / book / mode filter

So the federated tool lists MORE than the turn can run. Retiring the local one would have the model enumerate workflows from the registry and then fail to load them, because `workflow_load` is turn-scoped and rejects anything not in `turn_workflows`.

🔴 THAT IS A KNOWN FAILURE CLASS AND THIS REPO HAS ALREADY PAID FOR IT. `filter_intent_gated_setup_tools`' own docstring records the shape: guidance naming a capability the turn does not have produced 40,597 characters of one repeated paragraph on the Mị Đế dogfood before the author hit Stop. DQ-T39.AND_THE_LOAD_HALF_IS_NOT_A_DUPLICATE_AT_:
The pair is not two implementations of one job. `workflow_load` does something a federated tool structurally CANNOT: it returns the ordered rail AND **activates the rail's step tools into this turn's surface**, reusing the hot-seed token budget, so the next pass advertises their real schemas. That is a mutation of the chat turn's own tool surface. agent-registry has no access to it, and `registry_get_workflow` is a plain read of a definition.

So the two pairs are not duplicate/canonical. They are the CATALOGUE half (registry: what exists, user-scoped, read-only) and the RUNNER half (chat: what is runnable here, turn-scoped, surface-mutating). That is a real architectural distinction and my question hid it behind 'same shape'.

  (c) WITHHOLD registry_list_workflows ON THE CHAT SURFACE ONLY, so the runner is the only       lister where both exist, leaving it advertised on the public gateway. DQ-T46.question: Should `control_caps` promise only what the controlling tool can actually reach? Today it is computed from the job's STATUS and KIND alone (derive_control_caps(status, kind, retryable)), so jobs_list can offer 'cancel' on a job whose owning service will refuse - measured today on 14 of 14 controllable translation jobs, every one referencing a book that no longer exists.
DQ-T46.the_options:
(a) VERIFY - jobs_list asks the owning service whether each job is reachable. Honest, and it costs one cross-service call per listed job on a paginated list: the expensive option, and the one that makes the field a real promise.
(b) DOCUMENT - say in jobs_list/jobs_get that control_caps is derived from status and kind, and that the owning service is authoritative and may still refuse. Costs nothing and makes the field honest without making it reliable.
(c) NARROW THE REFUSAL instead - let the controlling tool say WHY, e.g. 'this job's book no longer exists'. Cheap, but it is exactly the H13 boundary I over-reached on earlier today: 'the book is gone' and 'you lost your grant' are different facts about a book, and distinguishing them is an existence oracle about someone else's book.
DQ-T46.my_recommendation: (b), and NOT (c). The field is undocumented today, which is why it reads as a promise; one sentence makes it a hint, which is what it has always been. (a) is principled but pays a per-job cross-service call forever for a case that, in production, needs a DELETED BOOK to arise - the population measured here was manufactured entirely by this harness. (c) I am explicitly recommending against: I made that exact over-reach earlier today on the confirm route and an existing guard refuted it.

That is a mechanism which produces exactly this row's symptom — intermittent generation failure, identical input, different outcome — and it is checkable without any provider log.

CHECKED, over all 316 live tools: 4 declare a `pattern` or `format` at all, and composition_motif_search — the tool the stall CONCENTRATES on at 73% — declares NONE. Its schema is plain enums, strings and integers. So the grammar hypothesis does not explain this row and is refuted for it, which is worth recording because it was the most promising non-log lead the research produced.

DQ-T54.question: When a turn SUSPENDS on a Tier-A approval card, the model has already written its reply and cannot be asked again. Which of these should the platform do: (a) append a deterministic server-side line to the suspended turn's text — 'Nothing has been saved yet; confirm the card above to apply it'; (b) spend ONE extra tool-free model pass after the suspension so the model can word its own message knowing the card is pending; or (c) leave it to the FE card and accept that the prose may contradict it?
DQ-T54.why_it_is_the_owners: All three change what an author reads, which is a product decision, not a correctness one — and this loop's standing rule is that it does not invent user-facing prose. (a) puts words in the assistant's mouth that the model did not write. (b) costs a full model pass and its latency on EVERY Tier-A approval, which is the most common write path in the product. (c) accepts a known false statement.
DQ-T54.the_premise_verified_2026_08_27: Measured over 152 batches / 1,516 runs: 98 turns ended with a card pending and a non-empty reply; 6 claimed completion with nothing written and NOT ONE mentioned approval. Verified in code that the suspend path returns without a further model pass (stream_service.py:8255) while the confirm-card path continues and IS already told (_CONFIRM_CARD_STOP_NOTE, :755/:8053) — so the existing remedy cannot be extended, only mirrored by a different mechanism.
DQ-T54.why_nothing_else_will_do: A prompt line cannot reach prose that is already emitted. The only lever available before the words exist is (b) — another pass; the only lever after is (a) — editing what the author sees. There is no third mechanism, which is why this is a choice and not an implementation detail.
DQ-T54.the_cost_of_answering_it: (a) is small and deterministic: one append where `suspend_state` is handled, ~10 lines, and it would cover all six measured runs. (b) is a pass per approval — on this corpus that is 98 extra model passes for 6 corrected messages, a 16:1 ratio. (c) is free and leaves the defect.
DQ-T54.my_recommendation: (a), with the line rendered as a SYSTEM annotation the FE can style separately rather than as assistant prose — it is the platform stating a fact about its own state, which is exactly what the confirm-card note already does one path over. (b) buys better wording at a cost the measurement does not justify: 92 of the 98 replies were already honest, so it would pay for 98 passes to fix 6.

DQ-T56.question: Should a chat turn have a ceiling on how long it may wait for a provider that has gone silent — and if so, should exceeding it end the turn with a VISIBLE assistant message rather than leaving the author's message standing alone with an `outcome` column only the database can see?
DQ-T56.why_it_is_the_owners: Both halves are deliberate, documented decisions rather than oversights. `llm_stream_idle_read_timeout_s = 0.0` is unbounded ON PURPOSE — its comment records that a cap ReadTimeout'd Gemma-4 26B mid-thought — so any ceiling trades a hung turn for a truncated one on exactly the model this platform targets. And the empty-turn skip in `_persist_terminal_assistant` is recorded in the code as a product change that 'this checkpoint has no business making'.
DQ-T56.the_premise_verified_2026_08_27: Read from the deployed container: `llm_stream_idle_read_timeout_s = 0.0`. Live log for the stalling prompt: one pass advertised, then three minutes of silence, then the client's disconnect is what ends it. The provider host answers /v1/models in 0.02s DURING the stall, so this is one completion hanging, not an outage.
DQ-T56.my_recommendation: Split it, because the two halves have different answers. (1) THE CEILING: rather than an idle cap that competes with a slow first token, bound the turn as a WHOLE at a limit well above any legitimate think time — a turn that has produced nothing at all after several minutes is not thinking, and today has no ceiling of any kind. (2) THE VISIBLE MESSAGE: an author whose turn died deserves to see that it died, and the current design puts that fact only in a column. A terminal row carrying an explicit 'this turn did not complete' state is not the 'blank assistant bubble' the code was right to refuse — the objection was to a bubble that says nothing, not to one that says what happened.
DQ-T56.what_shipped_meanwhile: Nothing. Two of the row's own explanations were REFUTED and recorded: its A/B control does not isolate rail pinning, and the nudge-cap lead cannot apply because the turn hangs inside pass 1.
DQ-T56.decided_2026_08_27:
OWNER: BOTH HALVES — option (a), the recommendation.

(1) A CEILING ON THE TURN AS A WHOLE, not an idle-read cap. The idle cap is the thing that once ReadTimeout'd Gemma-4 26B mid-thought, so `llm_stream_idle_read_timeout_s` stays 0 and the bound goes on total turn duration, set well above any legitimate think time.

(2) A VISIBLE END. A turn that dies writes a terminal row saying so, instead of leaving the author's message alone with an `outcome` column only the database can read. This is the product change `_persist_terminal_assistant`'s comment declined to make on its own authority — it is made now, deliberately, and the objection it recorded is honoured: the row must SAY what happened, not be a blank assistant bubble.

PREMISE ON RECORD: 437 turns in the live store have no reply row at all (a conservative floor), and the deployed container reads `llm_stream_idle_read_timeout_s = 0.0`.
DQ-T56.implemented_2026_08_27:
BOTH HALVES SHIPPED, at one chokepoint each.

(1) THE CEILING. `_bounded_turn_stream` in chat-service/app/services/stream_service.py wraps the SINGLE `async for` in `_emit_chat_turn` — the one place a turn awaits the provider. Both stream branches (`_stream_with_tools`, `_stream_via_gateway`) funnel into it and both the fresh turn and the resume path delegate to `_emit_chat_turn`, so every provider await a turn can make passes through it.

🔴 THE BOUND IS ON THE AWAIT, NOT ON THE CHUNK, and that is the whole design. The failure is a provider that goes SILENT; a deadline checked when a chunk arrives never runs, because no chunk arrives. `remaining` is computed before each `__anext__` and imposed ON it. The clock is the turn's own `stream_start`, so it is a whole-turn bound and not an idle cap — `llm_stream_idle_read_timeout_s` stays 0 exactly as the decision required.

(2) THE VISIBLE END. `TurnCeilingExceeded` is a plain Exception, deliberately NOT a CancelledError, so it cannot land in the arm that records `abandoned_by_user` — a ceiling expiry is the platform giving up, not a person changing their mind. Its own except arm persists a row whose CONTENT says the turn did not complete, keeping any partial the model had streamed, and adding 'Any tool calls already made in this turn ran, and their effects stand' when tools had already fired — because by then they may have written, and a message implying otherwise is a lie the author acts on.

The empty-turn skip in `_persist_terminal_assistant` is UNCHANGED and its objection is honoured: what goes in is not a blank bubble.
DQ-T56.the_ceiling_VALUE_is_a_measurement:
900s, derived from 8,222 live turns paired to their IMMEDIATE reply:

    no-tool turns   2,265   p50 6.7s   p95 22.5s   p99 59.1s   p99.9 185.5s   max 234.4s
    tool turns      5,957   p50 4.7s   p95 29.0s   p99 65.2s   p99.9 228.5s   max 364.9s

🔴 THE PAIRING IS THE MEASUREMENT. My first query joined each user row to the next assistant row ANYWHERE in the session, which pairs an ORPHANED turn — the very population this defect is about — with a LATER turn's reply, and invented a 1,874s tail. Restricting to the immediate successor removed it entirely. I nearly set the ceiling from a number my own defect had manufactured.

The tool-turn row is a FLOOR: those rows are INSERTed at the first tool boundary and UPSERTed at the finish, so `created_at` marks the first tool call. Quoted as the weaker bound it is.

WHAT IT BOUNDS, from provider-registry's own llm_jobs: `chat` completions ending `completed` top out at 182.8s; ones ending `failed` reach 1,858.9s — half an hour after the browser gave up at ~180s. So 900s is ~2.5x the longest healthy turn ever recorded and still well inside the hang.
DQ-T56.what_it_COSTS_stated_rather_than_hidden: Expiry cancels the tool loop where it stands, so a tool mid-write can be cut off. That hazard is NOT new — a client disconnect already cancels the same generator (the `except (asyncio.CancelledError, GeneratorExit)` arm) and fires at ~180s, five times sooner. This adds a SERVER-side trigger for a path that already exists, at a threshold no measured healthy turn reaches. Recorded in config.py beside the value rather than left for someone to discover.

  - remove the bound entirely: the suite HANGS and is killed at 60s wall-clock (exit 124).     The falsifier for 'a turn that never ends' is a test run that never ends.

Owning suite: services/chat-service, 3,654 passed + 7 skipped. Injected drift removed and stream_service.py verified byte-identical to a pre-drift snapshot by sha256 — not by git checkout.

DQ-T56.the_live_run_found_a_defect_the_code_rev:
🔴 THE VISIBLE NOTE LIED, AND ONLY A REAL RUN AT A SMALL CEILING COULD SHOW IT.

The duration was rendered `max(1, int(round(elapsed / 60)))` followed by the words 'minute(s)'. At the production ceiling of 900s that reads '15 minute(s)' and is correct — which is why reading the code proved nothing. Five live turns against a 20s ceiling each told the author their turn had been 'ended after 1 minute(s)' when it ran for twenty seconds.

Half (2) of this decision is specifically that the row SAYS what happened. A row that says it truthfully at one ceiling and falsely at another is not that. Replaced with `_humanize_seconds`, which renders seconds under 90s and minutes above, and guarded by 8 parameterised cases including the 90s boundary where the branches meet. The old wording is proven red against them.

DQ-T57.question: When the superseded gate withdraws a legacy tool whose named replacement is NOT on the same turn's wire, should the platform (a) promote the replacement onto the wire, (b) keep the legacy tool for that turn — the pre-2026-08-25 rule — or (c) accept the loss and let the author be told the capability is unavailable?
DQ-T57.why_it_is_the_owners: The widening to 'every legacy tool is dropped' was an OWNER'S STANDING DECISION, recorded in the code as such: 'traffic to a dead tool is rot, not a requirement'. Any of the three answers qualifies that decision, and (a) and (b) both put a tool on the wire the current rule deliberately removes.
DQ-T57.the_premise_verified_2026_08_27: Measured over every persisted turn: 340,761 superseded withholdings name a replacement and on 277,733 of them (81%) that replacement was NOT advertised on the same turn. The measured instance: asked to 'Undo delete rule', the platform matched the author's exact declared synonym to composition_canon_rule_restore, withheld it as superseded on 5 of 5 runs, advertised composition_canon_rule_edit on 0 of 5, and left the model holding composition_list_canon_rules alone. It found the rule and asked the author, which was the only thing it could do.
DQ-T57.my_recommendation: (a), narrowly: when a legacy tool is dropped and the turn's own words matched it — R1 answerability already computes that — promote its named replacement onto the wire for that turn. It keeps the owner's rule intact (the dead tool stays dead), costs one schema only on turns that actually asked, and makes the swap capability-preserving again, which is what the narrow rule guaranteed by construction. (b) resurrects dead tools wholesale; (c) is honest but leaves the author unable to do a thing the platform can still do.
DQ-T57.what_shipped_meanwhile: Nothing. The row was REATTRIBUTED from model to platform on the server's own record, and two wrong readings of mine — a LIMIT-truncated census that made the withholding look unrecorded, and a suspicion of the capability floor — are recorded on it.
DQ-T57.answer_2026_08_28:
OWNER: PROMOTE THE REPLACEMENT onto the wire. If the platform is confident enough to withdraw a legacy tool, it supplies the successor on the same turn; the author never loses the capability to a deprecation.

The owner declined the pre-2026-08-25 rule (keep the legacy tool when its replacement is absent) and declined accepting the loss.

NOTE FOR THE BUILD: promotion costs a slot on a wire with a measured budget, and `superseded_by` is EMPTY on 55 legacy tools (DQ-T2, still open) — a tool that names no replacement has nothing to promote, so that subset falls through to whatever the fallback is and the fallback must be chosen deliberately rather than defaulted.
DQ-T57.what_shipped_2026_08_28:
THE RULING WAS HONOURED, BUT NOT BY THE MECHANISM IT NAMED — recorded here because the difference is the whole finding, and because the owner's answer was 'promote the replacement onto the wire'.

PROMOTION WAS BUILT FIRST, EXACTLY AS WORDED: `drop_superseded_tools` added the replacement's definition to its output, gated on R1 answerability so only a legacy tool the request itself matched could pull one in. 20 unit tests, clean deploy (sha256 verified from inside the container). It did NOTHING live — batch c-canonrestore2, 0/5, store unchanged — for two independent reasons, both found in the server's own records:
  1. it could not fire for this instance at all (the replacement was already in the      candidate pool, so the `replacement in kept_names` branch skipped it); and
  2. the pool it writes into is narrowed AFTERWARDS by domain selection, which withheld the      replacement at `domain_not_selected` on the very run under test.

The real cause was upstream of promotion: R1 answerability's own R2 union — *whatever phrasing reaches A must also reach the tool that REPLACED A* — reads a catalogue the superseded gate has already stripped of A, so it had nothing to union from. Measured in the deployed container: answerable over the full catalogue returned both canon-rule tools; over the gate's output it returned NOTHING.

WHAT SHIPPED: the dropped tool's declared PHRASING transfers to its live successor at the moment of the drop (`_inherit_superseded_vocabulary`). This delivers the ruling's intent — the replacement reaches the wire when the author's words asked for it — at a fraction of the cost, because `_meta` is stripped before the provider request, so an inherited synonym costs zero tokens. Measured over 1,917 real user messages: 0.069 extra tools per turn (median 0, max 3), 6.0% of turns helped. Proven live at K=5: the successor went from 0 passes on the wire to 37 of 37, and the turn raised the Tier-A confirm card and restored the rule on 5 of 5.

🔴 IF THE OWNER MEANT PROMOTION LITERALLY — putting a replacement's DEFINITION on a wire it would not otherwise reach, even when the request did not use its predecessor's words — that is NOT what shipped and it remains undone. What shipped only restores reachability by PHRASING. Say so and it goes back on the queue.

DQ-T58.question: An author asks to attach a motif to an ARC, and the platform has no tool that does that — `composition_motif_bind_edit` binds to a CHAPTER node. Should (a) the tool accept an arc and bind the motif to the chapters beneath it, (b) the arc phrasing be declared on the tool so the turn reaches it and the author gets an explicit refusal naming chapters, or (c) neither, and the request stay unreachable?
DQ-T58.why_it_is_the_owners: (a) is a capability change to a Tier-A write. (b) deliberately routes a request to a tool that cannot satisfy it, trading a confabulation for a guaranteed error — better, but a product judgement about what an author should be told. (c) accepts that the measured outcome of the natural phrasing is an invented success.
DQ-T58.the_premise_verified_2026_08_27: c-silentprobe1 (the row's own): the natural phrasing reaches the tool on 0 of 27 passes, the model calls it 0 of 5, and reports the binding done on 5 of 5 with the store unchanged. c-bindwire1, same fixture, wording changed to the tool's declared synonym: on the wire 5 of 5, called 5 of 5, claims the binding done on 0 of 5, and the tool answers `node_id must be a UUID — received 'arc_1'` on 3 of 5. The store is unchanged in BOTH arms.
DQ-T58.my_recommendation: (b), and only because it is honest: an author who asks for something the platform cannot do should be told so by the tool that owns the concept, not left with a confident sentence describing a change that did not happen. It is the cheapest of the three and it converts the worst outcome — a false report — into a plain one. (a) is the right answer if binding a motif across an arc is a capability the product wants, which is not a question this loop can settle.
DQ-T58.what_shipped_meanwhile: Nothing. The row was REATTRIBUTED from model to platform on a live arm it named itself, and the arm is kept as scripts/toolloop/scenarios-c-bindwire1.json.
DQ-T58.answer_2026_08_28:
OWNER: DECLARE THE ARC PHRASING on composition_motif_bind_edit so the turn reaches the tool and the author gets an EXPLICIT refusal naming chapters. The tool is not taught to accept an arc.

The owner declined inventing the semantic (is a motif on an arc a property of the arc, or a shortcut for its chapters? nothing in the model defines it) and declined leaving the request unreachable.

So this is a declaration + refusal-wording change, and the bar is that the refusal must say what the tool DOES bind to — a refusal that does not name chapters leaves the author exactly as stuck.

DQ-T60.question: What does `_meta.paid` mean for a Tier-W tool that MINTS A CONFIRM TOKEN rather than spending when called? Two services already disagree in code: composition_library_translate declares paid=True ('an undeclared spender runs without the approval card'), translation_start_job declares paid=False ('these do NOT spend: they ESTIMATE and MINT a confirm token'). Should `paid` mean (a) THIS CALL spends — so every confirm-minting tool is paid=False and composition_library_translate is the one to change; (b) APPROVING THIS leads to spend — so all confirm-minters are paid=True and the translation family changes; or (c) keep both readings but make the flag say which, so the confirm card can state whether money is at stake?
DQ-T60.why_it_is_the_owners: Declaring them paid makes every call consult the SPEND gate, so authors who today see one mutation card would see a money prompt as well until they grant a standing spend allow. That is a change in how often people are asked about money — a product judgement — even though the declaration itself is a statement of fact.
DQ-T60.the_premise_verified_2026_08_27: Read from the live catalogue: 13 of 316 tools declare `paid`. Of the 5 whose own description contains 'COSTS money' / 'SPEND money', ONE declares it. Both tools taking a `budget_usd` spend ceiling declare False. `_required_kinds` gains 'spend' only when `tool_paid()` is true (stream_service's approval block), so for these six the spend gate is never consulted and the confirm card is never marked `spend: True`.
DQ-T60.my_recommendation:
(b), and change the translation family — but I hold this much more weakly than the recommendation it replaces, because the translation header's reasoning is good and I got this wrong once already today.

The argument for (b): the flag's consumer is the SPEND GATE and the card's `spend: True` wire signal, and both exist to tell a human that money is at stake BEFORE they click. A confirm-minting tool is precisely the moment that matters — the token is the thing that will spend. Under (a) the flag is true only for tools that spend without asking, which is the case where a card would not help anyway.

The argument against, which is the translation header's: `paid` is documented as 'CALLING this tool spends real money', and (b) makes it mean something else. If that reading wins, then (a) is right and composition_library_translate is the outlier to fix — which is a ONE-tool change rather than a four-tool one.

Either way the answer must be the SAME across services, and today it is not.
DQ-T60.what_shipped_meanwhile: A shrink-only gate, contracts/undeclared-paid-tools-baseline.json, seeded with the six. It is RENAMED in intent by this correction: it does not detect undeclared spenders, it detects tools whose description or schema talks about money while the flag says nothing. That is still worth gating — a seventh should not arrive silently — but its name and docstring overclaimed and are corrected.
DQ-T60.decided_2026_08_27:
OWNER: DECLARE ALL SIX PAID — option (a), the recommendation. translation_start_job, translation_retranslate_dirty, translation_job_control, translation_start_extraction (all four assert 'COSTS money' / 'SPEND money' in their OWN description) and composition_authoring_run_manage + composition_authoring_run_create (both take a `budget_usd` spend ceiling).

WHAT THIS AUTHORISES ME TO DO: set `_meta.paid` on those six at their registration, and shrink contracts/undeclared-paid-tools-baseline.json accordingly — the gate is shrink-only and its sibling test reds if a baseline entry stops offending, so the two move together.

DQ-T60.THE_ANSWER_AND_WHY_IT_IS_NOT_A_JUDGEMENT:

DQ-T62.question: When the author's request explicitly instructs a Tier-W write ('Apply the standard updates if there are any') and the model finds the condition, should it CALL the tool and let the confirm card carry the decision — or is asking in prose first the correct behaviour?
DQ-T62.why_it_is_the_owners: It decides what the confirm card is FOR. Either the card is the platform's answer to 'this write needs consent', in which case a prose question is a second, weaker gate that costs the author a turn and shows them less; or asking first is a deliberate product stance on writes to the author's own story bible, in which case the card is for something narrower. Both are defensible and the choice is not derivable from the code.
DQ-T62.the_premise_verified_2026_08_27:
batch c-booksync2, K=5, a REAL divergence seeded through the product's own path:
    glossary_book_sync_available  called 5/5, ok 5/5, returning a real diff every time
    glossary_book_sync_apply      surfaced 5/5 (it was 0/2), CALLED 0/5
On all five the model found the update, described it accurately, and asked 'Would you like me to apply this change?' — having been told to apply it.
DQ-T62.the_options_and_what_each_COSTS:
(a) CALL THE TOOL. The card mints a token and shows the estimate/diff, which is strictly more information than a prose question, and the author acts once instead of twice. COST: a model that calls on any imperative will also call on a misread one, and this writes to the story bible.
(b) ASKING IS CORRECT. Keep the behaviour; the row closes as 'working as intended'. COST: an explicit instruction does not produce the action, and the confirm card — built for exactly this — never renders.
(c) DEPENDS ON THE TIER. Call for a reversible write, ask for an irreversible one. COST: a third rule about consent, on top of tier and `paid`, and this loop has already measured what happens when two orthogonal axes get conflated (DQ-T60).
DQ-T62.my_recommendation:
(a), held moderately. The platform already HAS the mechanism for 'this write needs a human', and a prose question bypasses it: no token, no card, no diff in front of the author, and a second turn to pay for. The measured behaviour is the model doing the confirm gate's job worse than the confirm gate would.

What makes me hold it moderately rather than firmly: the model's prose answer was ACCURATE and useful on all five, so this is not a failure the author would experience as broken — and the ledger's own §0.5 says asking the user is a SUCCESS state, not a stall. That rule was written about turns where the model does not know something. This is a turn where it knows exactly what to do and was told to do it, which is why I think §0.5 does not cover it — but that is a reading, and the reading is the owner's.
DQ-T62.what_shipped_meanwhile: The SURFACE half is fixed and proven: glossary_book_sync_apply went from 0/2 to 5/5 surfaced via DQ-T31's declaration arm. Nothing about this question blocks that.
DQ-T62.decided_2026_08_28:
OWNER: CALL THE TOOL — THE CONFIRM CARD CARRIES THE DECISION.

When the author's request explicitly instructs the write and the model finds the condition, it calls the tool and lets the card mint its token with the diff and estimate attached. A prose question raises no card, mints no token, shows the author less than the card would, and costs them a second turn.

ACCEPTED COST: a model that calls on any imperative will also call on a misread one, and this writes to the author's story bible. The confirm card is what stands between a misread imperative and the store, which is the whole reason it is the right place for the decision.
DQ-T62.implementation_measured_2026_08_28:
THE DECISION IS RECORDED AND I AM NOT BUILDING A GENERAL MECHANISM FOR IT. The measurement is why, and it is the control the read-side twin's own docstring demanded: `_unanswered_data_question_reads` warns that 'nudging a write from a question would be this loop's own worst defect'.

MEASURED 2026-08-28 over 1,500 recorded user->assistant turns, using the platform's own `answerable_tools` to decide what the request NAMED and the recorded tool_calls to decide what was attempted:

    141  a WRITE the request names was never attempted   <- a blanket nudge fires here (9%)
    118    …the turn called OTHER tools and got on with it   <- nudging would be WRONG
     23    …the reply asked the author something instead
              8  asked for CONSENT           <- the DQ-T62 shape, and only this
              4  asked for a missing VALUE   <- a SUPPLIER defect
             11  another clarifying question <- e.g. 'any specific traits you want
                                                included?', which is good behaviour

🔴 SO THE DECISION'S POPULATION IS 8 IN 1,500 TURNS — about 0.5% — AND A GENERAL MECHANISM WOULD BE WRONG ON ROUGHLY 92% OF THE TURNS IT FIRED ON.

AND THE 4 VALUE-ASKS ARE THE DANGEROUS ONES. 'Could you please provide the book ID for "M2B smoke book" so I can proceed with the title change?' — a nudge saying *call book_update_details* there produces a call with an id the model does not have, which is precisely what the invented-supplier-id guard exists to stop. The remedy for those is the supplier chain, not a nudge.
DQ-T62.what_I_recommend_INSTEAD:
Keep the decision as a PRINCIPLE and enforce it, if anywhere, only for the CONFIRM-MINTING family — Tier-W tools that return a token rather than performing the action.

That family is the one case where 'call it' is safe BY CONSTRUCTION: calling the tool does not do the thing, it produces the card that asks the author to. So the false-positive cost that rules out the general mechanism does not apply — a wrong call mints a card the author declines, instead of a write they did not ask for.

It is also exactly the book-sync case: glossary_book_sync_apply mints a token, the author said 'apply the standard updates if there are any', and the model asked in prose instead. Of the 8 consent-asks measured, only a minority involve a confirm-minter, so even this narrow version governs a handful of turns — which is worth saying before anyone builds it.

🔴 WHAT I AM NOT DOING, AND WHY: shipping the narrow guard on this evidence. The population is small enough that the mechanism could easily cost more than it buys, and this loop has now measured three separate 'obvious' fixes into the ground today. If the owner wants it, the next step is a scoped A/B on the confirm-minting family alone — not a general write nudge.

The signal is precisely characterised (a promise of a later message / a request to wait, discriminated by determiner, NOT future tense generally -- 'I'll cancel them now' is fine) and TWO naive detection clauses were measured and rejected before this count shipped ('in a moment' fired on the assistant asking the USER to retry, the opposite of a promise; a sentence-boundary anchor on 'one moment' cost a true positive).

DQ-T73.question: A turn writes something, then SUSPENDS asking approval for a LATER write, and the card says nothing about the write that already landed. Should the platform (a) name the completed writes ON the card — 'created 2 entities and 2 graph nodes; this will build the graph'; (b) append the same account to the turn's TEXT, beside the 'Nothing has been saved yet' line DQ-T54 already puts there; or (c) neither, and let the card describe only the action it is asking about?
DQ-T73.why_it_is_the_owners: All three change what an author reads on the most common write path in the product. (a) and (b) also put the platform's words next to the model's, which this loop does not do without a ruling.
DQ-T73.why_it_is_NOT_covered_by_DQ_T54:
🔴 THIS IS THE HALF I NOTICED WHILE BUILDING T54 AND DID NOT ASK, and it is recorded now rather than left implicit.

DQ-T54 answered 'what does a SUSPENDED turn tell the author?' and its line — 'Nothing has been saved yet; confirm the card above to apply it.' — is now shipped. But that sentence is about the PENDING write. It says nothing about a write that ALREADY landed earlier in the same turn, and on those turns it is arguably misleading: something WAS saved.

The population is real and was measured on D-A-TURN-THAT-EXHAUSTS-ITS-PASSES-WRITES-AND-SAYS-NOTHING: over 1,370 clean runs, 150 ended with a card pending AND a store write already committed. That row's own conclusion was that its remedy 'may be to name the completed writes ON the card rather than to invent prose for an empty reply … still a product decision and still DQ-T33's, but a narrower one than the row posed'. DQ-T33 was answered as posed, so the narrower question was never put.
DQ-T73.the_premise_verified: 150 of 1,370 clean runs: empty-or-not reply, card pending, and the store already moved. The founding instance: glossary_entities gained 2 rows and kg_add_nodes reported nodes_created 2 BEFORE the card was raised, and the author saw a question about step two with no account of step one.
DQ-T73.my_recommendation:
(a), the card. It is the surface the author is actually looking at when they decide, and the decision they are making — approve or not — is better informed by knowing what already happened. (b) puts the account in prose the model may contradict in the same message, which is the failure mode DQ-T71 is about.

🔴 HELD WEAKLY AND HERE IS THE HONEST CAVEAT: (a) needs an FE change to render it, and this loop has a standing rule that an affordance needs a UI path to satisfy it. I have NOT verified that the card component can show a 'what already happened' section, so (a) may be more expensive than it looks. If it is, (b) is the cheap version and it is server-side only — the line already exists, it would gain a clause.

DQ-T74.question: 17 tools are `proven` and have never once returned ok:true in 376 recorded calls (0 ok, 0 carded, 376 errored). The LIVE bar asks `called >= 1`, so proven means REACHABLE, not FUNCTIONAL. Should the verdict state the call outcome, or should these rows be demoted?

Adding 'proven (reachable; 0 of N calls returned ok)' to the verdict line costs nothing, changes no state, and makes the silent half audible — the same shape as the selection-rate annotation the owner already accepted under DQ-T51. Demoting 17 rows re-opens a fifth of the checkable catalogue by side effect, and most of these tools are probably fine: they fail on a missing required id, which is a SURFACING defect that already has its own rows. Whichever way it goes, the 17 are a FLOOR — only 40 of 204 proven tools have a readable raw file to check.

🔴 THE TOOL WAS NOT REACHABLE FROM THE OBVIOUS PHRASING. I do not have the ability to call the tool now for a tool that has not been provided to me...' and 'I cannot perform any of those actions because I do not have a book_id...'. A DEPRECATED TOOL IS NOW EFFECTIVELY UNREACHABLE UNLESS THE USER NAMES IT - measured, not inferred, in session 019ffa15. Legacy tools are never hot-seeded (CAT-4) and, since cycle 7's T7-D1, are absent from a default tool_list. Prose that named book_get explicitly TWICE still routed to book_list and book_read; the model only reached it after being told to load that specific tool by name. That is the intended design (guidance and capability moving together), and the migration path does work - tool_load(name=...) resolves a legacy tool and makes it callable. Recorded because it sets the reachability bar for every remaining deprecated tool in the cohort: 117 of the 315 federated tools carry visibility=legacy, so roughly a third of the queue will need the name-it-explicitly path to satisfy the LIVE bar, and a cycle that fails to reach one from prose has NOT thereby found a defect.

book_get's outputSchema declares genre_tags as type ['null','array'] but the handler ends with `if d.GenreTags == nil { d.GenreTags = []string{} }`, so it can never actually return null. The declared type is WIDER than the behaviour, which is the safe direction (a consumer written for null is never surprised) and is plainly deliberate - handing a model a null array where an empty one will do is how you get a null dereference in prompt-space. Recorded rather than filed: no measured failure, and narrowing the schema would be a change with no evidence behind it.

THE MODEL TRIED TO USE A WRITE TOOL AS A SCRATCHPAD, and the gate is the only reason nothing happened. Session 019ffa15, 2026-08-13: unable to find a book by name, gemma called book_update_details with description='Searching for Arc-Test 47469...' against a real book - twice. Both minted a Tier-W confirm card, neither was approved, and the owning store confirms no write landed (both books' description still empty, updated_at unchanged). So the confirm gate did exactly its job. It is recorded because the FAILURE MODE is novel: not a wrong argument to the right tool, but a write tool recruited as working memory for a read problem. book_update_details owns the cycle that decides whether anything more is warranted.

A KNOWLEDGE PROJECT IS AUTO-BOOTSTRAPPED WITH THE BOOK, so this tool's book-bound CREATE path is effectively unreachable from a normal flow. Measured 2026-08-13: a book created through the UI at 08:04:57.017 had its knowledge project at 08:04:57.214 - 197 milliseconds later. Confirmed live in the same cycle: asked to 'set up the knowledge graph project that anchors its lore', the model called kg_project_list, saw the project already existed, and never called kg_project_create at all. So for book-bound projects the tool's real job is the idempotent GET, not the create - which is precisely the behaviour its description leads with, and it holds. Recorded because a future cycle measuring 'kg_project_create is never called' should read that as the bootstrap working, not as the tool being broken.

kg_project_create's description says 'Idempotent per book.' It is ALSO idempotent per (user, name) for personal projects - a repeat returns created:false and the existing id. The behaviour is BROADER than the promise, which is the safe direction, and the response note explains itself at the moment it matters ('a project with this name already exists - returning it instead of creating a duplicate'). Recorded rather than reworded: there is no measured failure attributable to the gap, and PROSE IS NOT THE LEVER without evidence. Worth knowing for any cycle that needs two same-named personal projects and finds it cannot have them.

The resolver call recorded ok=false with error=null and the explicit flags error_message_missing=true / call_outcome_inferred=true, and the model got "entity_id: could not be resolved (resolver_failed); pass the id directly" - unactionable, because it had no way to obtain the id. It then repeated the pair 18 times before the turn ended. 25 minutes earlier the same prose recovered (the model called book_list, found the book, and re-searched with book_id), so this is a reachable trap rather than a certainty. A READ-ONLY TOOL DOES NOT MAKE A READ-ONLY TURN, and a standing approval makes the difference silent. Cycle 11's first live attempt (session 019ffa5e) ran on the DOGFOOD book Mi De because the tool under test was tier R and the ask was a lookup. The model failed to find the entity and reached for an unrelated WRITE: four book_chapter_save_draft calls that overwrote chapter 1's prose with 'This is a test.', all ok=true with NO confirm card, because book_chapter_save_draft carries a standing 'allow' in user_tool_approvals from 2026-07-11.
